procedural_history.originating_court: Illaqa/Duty Magistrate, Kurukshetra (directed registration of FIR)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 11.02.2016 of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M No. 35679 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused filed an application (CRM-M No. 35679 of 2014) before the High Court to quash the FIR, arguing the dispute was civil in nature. The High Court quashed the proceedings arising out of the FIR, stating the complainant failed to demonstrate criminal intent on the part of the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The complainant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing the High Court erred in exercising its power under Section 482 CrPC, especially after a chargesheet was filed and charges were framed. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and clarified that it expressed no opinion on the merits of the accusation, which is a subject matter of the criminal trial.

directions: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order of the High Court dated 11.2.2016 is set aside.
It is clarified that no opinion has been expressed on the merits of the accusation which is a subject matter of the criminal trial.
Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to quash an FIR and the subsequent criminal proceedings on the ground that the complainant had failed to establish any criminal intent on the part of the accused.

facts: An FIR was registered against the accused for offenses including cheating (S. 420 IPC) and forgery, based on a property sale agreement.
The complainant alleged that they were induced to pay a significant amount of money (Rs. 10 lakhs) to the accused for the property.
The High Court quashed the FIR, reasoning that a plain reading of the complaint showed only a refusal to execute the sale deed, which did not establish any criminal intent.
However, the police investigation, which occurred before the High Court's decision, revealed a crucial fact: the accused allegedly did not have title to the property she was attempting to sell.
By the time the High Court quashed the proceedings, a chargesheet had already been filed and charges had been framed against the accused.
law: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to quash criminal proceedings should be exercised sparingly.
In deciding whether to quash an FIR, a court should not limit its review to the initial complaint alone but must also consider crucial aspects that emerge during the investigation.
The question of whether allegations are true or false is a matter to be determined during a full criminal trial, not in a preliminary proceeding under Section 482 CrPC.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court made a significant error by focusing solely on the FIR and ignoring key findings from the police investigation.

The High Court concluded there was no criminal intent based on the simple fact that the vendor refused to complete the sale. It overlooked the more serious allegation, uncovered during the investigation, that the accused was selling a property she did not own.

The Supreme Court reasoned that this allegation—that the accused dealt with a property without having title and induced the complainant to part with money on that basis—was a strong indicator of potential criminal intent from the outset.

The Court held that the correctness of this serious allegation was a matter of evidence and had to be decided at trial. The High Court was not justified in pre-judging the issue and quashing the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was not justified in quashing the criminal proceedings. The High Court had improperly ignored crucial facts that emerged during the investigation, specifically the allegation that the accused did not have title to the property she agreed to sell. The Supreme Court ruled that this allegation pointed to a potential criminal intent that deserved to be examined in a full trial, and therefore, it set aside the High Court's order and allowed the criminal proceedings to continue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to quash an FIR and the subsequent criminal proceedings on the ground that the complainant had failed to establish any criminal intent on the part of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC to quash the proceedings, particularly after an investigation had been conducted, a chargesheet filed, and charges framed.
Criminal intent is evident from the fact that the accused attempted to sell a property they did not own, and through this transaction, induced the appellant to part with valuable consideration.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not appear before the Supreme Court.

The arguments that succeeded in the High Court, forming the basis of the respondent's position, were that the dispute was of a civil nature and that the FIR, by only indicating a refusal to execute a sale deed, failed to establish any criminal intent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court is not justified in exercising its power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash criminal proceedings when crucial facts supporting the allegations have emerged during the course of an investigation, as the veracity of such allegations is a matter to be determined at trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in quashing the criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC because it improperly limited its analysis to the contents of the FIR. The High Court ignored crucial facts that emerged during the investigation, specifically the allegation that the accused attempted to sell a property to which she did not have title, thereby inducing the complainant to part with valuable consideration.
legal_tests_applied: The power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC should not be exercised when crucial facts supporting the criminal allegations have emerged during the investigation, subsequent to the filing of the FIR.

The determination of the truth or falsity of allegations, particularly after a chargesheet has been filed and charges have been framed, is a matter to be decided at trial, not in a summary proceeding for quashing an FIR.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court's reasoning, upon which the respondent's case rested, was flawed because it focused exclusively on the FIR's statement that the vendor refused to execute the sale deed.
The High Court incorrectly concluded there was no criminal intent by failing to consider crucial aspects that emerged during the investigation, which went beyond the initial FIR.
The argument that the dispute was purely civil in nature was undermined by the investigation's finding that the accused allegedly did not have title to the property she was selling.
why_respondent_won: The High Court erred by losing sight of crucial facts that emerged during the investigation, which occurred after the FIR was filed but before the quashing order was passed.

The complainant's core allegation, supported by the investigation, was that the accused induced him to part with money by dealing with a property to which she lacked title, which prima facie suggests criminal intent.

The Supreme Court held that the correctness of the allegations is a matter for trial, and it was inappropriate for the High Court to usurp the trial court's function, especially after a chargesheet had been filed and charges framed.
policy_considerations: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised sparingly and not to stifle a legitimate prosecution where investigation has revealed a prima facie case.

The merits of a criminal accusation, including the truthfulness of allegations and the existence of criminal intent, should be determined through the process of a full trial rather than a summary judgment at the initial stage.
